transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Tomás Ríos (Hearthstone CTO), Aisha Khan (Head of Platform), Ben Carter (DevOps)

Summary:
Quick kickoff for Hearthstone Data's pilot with Redwood. Align on network/VPC requirements, compliance items (SOC2, SSO), pilot scope (1 model, inference latency targets), and next steps for a pre-prod connectivity test.

Topics:
- VPC peering and network prep
- Data residency and retention
- Pilot success criteria and metrics (latency, cost, error rate)
- Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs
- Security docs and SSO/KMS integration

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood. We have Maya from SE; we'll walk through the kickoff, network, and SLA items.
[00:18] Tomás Ríos: Hey Jordan, great to meet you. We just grabbed a quick slot before our sprint retro. Trying to get the pilot in week two.
[00:24] Maya Chen: Hi Tomas, hi Aisha and Ben — quick intro from me, I'm Maya, focus on infra and performance. We'll want to understand your traffic shape and security constraints.
[00:35] Aisha Khan: Hi, quick context — Hearthstone handles analytics for financial customers; regulatory stuff is part of the ask. We care about audit logs and encryption at rest.
[00:44] Ben Carter: Also network — we're behind a strict firewall. Need to know peering details and if Redwood supports private link or similar.
[00:52] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support VPC peering and private connectors in several regions. For private deployment we have both VPC and on-prem options, though on-prem is heavier lift.
[01:05] Tomás Ríos: The SOC2 question — do you have the compliance pack and can we get evidence for our auditors?
[01:12] Maya Chen: We can share SOC2 type II summary, our security whitepaper, and specifics around audit logs. We'll note that some transcriptions sometimes say "Redwood Dedicate" — that's an artifact, but the product is Redwood Dedicated / Hosted.
[01:26] Ben Carter: Cool. For networking, we need the exact CIDR and ports. Also curious about latency expectations — our SLAs are tight, we aim for p99 under 120ms for chat endpoints.
[01:38] Jordan Lee: For small sequence lengths, hosted endpoints often meet that, but p99 depends on batching and workload. Dedicated pools give more predictable latency. There's also caching — prefix/KV cache — that can shave token latency but depends on your pattern.
[01:52] Aisha Khan: How does cost look for dedicated vs hosted for our expected volume? We have sporadic spikes during close-of-business runs.
[02:01] Maya Chen: Dedicated is a reserved capacity model — predictable but requires commit. Hosted is pay-as-you-go; for spikes we have autoscale / burst policies. We can model your expected monthly token consumption in the worksheet I'll send.
[02:18] Tomás Ríos: On data handling: we need to ensure customer PII is not logged or saved. Can we set retention to zero and hold logs in our KMS?
[02:27] Maya Chen: You can enable customer-managed KMS for keys in private deployments; for Hosted, we offer encryption at rest and options to redact logs. We'll pull the exact retention and redact controls into the runbook.
[02:39] Ben Carter: For SSO, do you support SAML/SCIM? We need RBAC tied to our IdP.
[02:45] Jordan Lee: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported; we also have RBAC roles in the console.
[02:51] Aisha Khan: Also network egress — some of our data can't leave EU. Any region-level residency?
[02:58] Maya Chen: We have region deployments in NA and EU; for stricter residency we recommend the private deployment in your region. There are on-prem variants too but that's more involved.
[03:09] Tomás Ríos: For the pilot scope — proposing one model for semantic search + embeddings and a small generation endpoint for summaries. Success metrics: embeddings QoR on our eval set, p95 latency under 80ms, cost under $X per 1k requests.
[03:28] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. For embeddings caching and batching we can recommend settings that reduce cost. We'll also propose a quantization profile if you want lower GPU usage.
[03:38] Ben Carter: One more — we want to run a short throughput test. Can Redwood spin up a temporary dedicated pool for that or do we do it on hosted?
[03:46] Maya Chen: We can run benchmarks on hosted but for deterministic throughput we'd mirror on a small dedicated pool in a trial arrangement. I'll note that as a follow-up.
[03:54] Tomás Ríos: Any blockers on our side before the 1/12 smoke test?
[03:59] Ben Carter: We'll need the CIDR and port list, and a security contact. Also will need the onboarding IAM role or temp credentials.
[04:09] Jordan Lee: We'll send a network prep checklist with CIDR, port ranges, and peering instructions. Also include a template for the IAM role and a sample security contact email.
[04:20] Aisha Khan: Regarding audit logs, do we get token-level traces for latency breakdowns? We need to trace per-request token counts and cost.
[04:29] Maya Chen: Yes, the console has per-token cost and latency breakdown; token traces can be included in logs, and we've exported examples in our observability docs.
[04:38] Tomás Ríos: Great. Let's talk timeline: we want pilot live within two weeks. Is that realistic?
[04:44] Jordan Lee: Realistic if we get VPC info and accounts set up this week. We'll aim for a pre-prod connectivity test on 1/12, then a short pilot window 1/13-1/20.
[04:55] Ben Carter: Regarding service-levels, what's the escalation path if we see errors during the pilot?
[05:00] Maya Chen: SE will be primary contact — that's me — and we have an on-call infra team. For Dedicated, enterprise customers get a higher touch SLA with phone escalation.
[05:10] Tomás Ríos: Any limitations around model versions or quantization? We may want 4-bit quant for cost.
[05:16] Maya Chen: We support quantization-friendly execution paths and multiple kernels. For some models, 4-bit quant can affect quality; we'll include recommended quant profiles for your workload. We'll flag when quality regression risk is present.
[05:28] Jordan Lee: Also wanted to flag competitors — you mentioned evaluating Anthropic and Vertex; we can share benchmark comparisons relevant to your use-case though it's high-level.
[05:36] Aisha Khan: Helpful. We also heard about a vendor called Infranode from a partner — any pitfalls?
[05:40] Maya Chen: Infranode does on-prem inference; tradeoffs are similar — more control but more ops. Redwood's differentiator is unified tooling across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.
[05:52] Ben Carter: Ok, security: can we get a copy of the controls matrix and a sample DPA?
[05:57] Jordan Lee: Yes, will include SOC2, controls matrix, and a template DPA.
[06:05] Tomás Ríos: Perfect. Any caveats about burst traffic and autoscaling? We have budget constraints.
[06:11] Maya Chen: Autoscale helps for spikes but can increase cost; we can define burst caps. For cost-sensitive workloads we recommend caching, batching, and tailored quant profiles.
[06:23] Aisha Khan: On governance — we'll need role separation and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[06:29] Maya Chen: We support log forwarding and syslog/S3 exports. We'll include a sample ETL for the SIEM.
[06:37] Jordan Lee: Recap then: we'll send runbook, network checklist, SOC2 and controls, pilot config template, and schedule the 1/12 smoke test.
[06:45] Tomás Ríos: Sounds good. Ben will provide the CIDR and security contact by 1/6.
[06:50] Ben Carter: Yep I'll get that.
[06:53] Jordan Lee: Any other questions?
[06:55] Aisha Khan: Not on my side, thanks.
[06:57] Maya Chen: Quick note — sometimes transcripts mung model names, e.g., "KV cache" shows as "K V cash" in auto transcripts, ignore those.
[07:07] Jordan Lee: Thanks all. We'll follow up via email with the attachments.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: some speaker attributions may be imperfect; punctuation and proper nouns may be off in a few places (e.g., product names).
